title: stochastic-fusion-exercise-notes
body:
Purpose: quick exploratory playbook for stochastic/fuzzy probing of fused-op vs. FlashAttention vs. paged-backed attention across mixed-sequence workloads. Aim is narrow: find low-effort kernel-decision heuristics that reduce p99 tail without regressing steady-state throughput.

Background/context:
- Recent customer load with many short chat turns + occasional long context (up to 4k) shows spiky p99 on H100 clusters.
- Hypothesis: kernel handoffs + prefetch thrash on mixed seqlen mixes cause microstutters. Fused-op paths are great when they stay hot; FlashAttention better for long sequences when memory locality holds. Paged-backed attention avoids OOM but may induce extra copy overhead.

Quick experiment matrix (run on h100-gpu-2, CUDA 12.2):
- Models: gpt2-medium (12B-like perf proxy), llama-13b-16k (dense kernel exercise)
- Kernels: flash, paged, fusedops, hybrid-fallback (our runtime's on-the-fly switch)
- Seq mixes: short-heavy (80% 32/20% 128), mixed (50/30/20 -> 16/128/1024), long-spike (95% 64, 5% 4096)
- Batches: 1, 8, 32 (simulate inference ladder)
- Metrics: tokens/sec (steady), p50/p95/p99 latency (ms per request), kernel-switch counts, GPU memcpy counts, CPU-side scheduling stalls (ms), page-faults if any.

Commands used (dev harness):
python -m bench.attn_run --model gpt2-medium --seq-mix "32:0.8,128:0.2" --batch-sizes 1,8,32 --kernels flash,fused,paged,hybrid --profile --trace=traceplay_$(date +%s).nsys
(artifact collection: nvtx + Nsight systems + runtime trace logs under /tmp/attn_play/)

Representative results (summary):
- Short-heavy, batch=8: fusedops best steady throughput (tokens/sec +12% vs flash), p99=18ms vs flash p99=26ms. Kernel switch rate low.
- Mixed, batch=8: hybrid-fallback yields best p99 (28ms) by avoiding late fallback storms; fusedops p99=45ms due to occasional fallback to slower tiled path when a 1024 sequence arrives mid-batch. Flash p99=60ms because of transient memory pressure and prefetch thrash.
- Long-spike, batch=1: FlashAttention wins for single long request (tokens/sec higher, p99 lower) but causes brief GC-like memory reclamation that increases subsequent short-request p99 by ~35ms unless KV cache warmup allowed.

Telemetry notes observed in traces:
- Kernel handshake latency spike correlates with 'kv-alloc' events at ~24ms when long seq enters node.
- CUDA memcpy peaks align with paged path on long spikes; paged reduces peak GPU mem but increases PCIe traffic.
- Scheduler log shows queue re-ordering (our micro-batcher tries to coalesce but drops to FIFO when hybrid-fallback toggles), producing small head-of-line blocking.

Quick hypotheses (ranked):
1) Reduce kernel handoff frequency by hysteresis on fallback (require sustained seqlen signal for N consecutive requests before switching).
2) Introduce ephemeral pre-warming for KV cache when a long request is detected but keep it limited-time to avoid memory blowup.
3) Bias the micro-batcher to prefer short-request fast-path packing when overload detected (sacrifices a few long-request tokens/sec for overall p99).

Micro-experiment to validate hypothesis 1 (hysteresis):
- Config patch: fallback_hysteresis.window=3 (must see 3 long seqs in a row to switch), fallback_hysteresis.cooldown=10s.
- Result: on mixed load, kernel switches dropped 78%, p99 improved from 45ms to 29ms, steady throughput -2%.
- Cost: slight increased latency for first long-request but better global tail.

Notes about instrumentation improvements needed:
- Add lightweight kernel-switch counters exported to prometheus (label by model+seqlen-bin+node).
- Emit nvtx ranges for 'kv-alloc' and 'kernel-handshake' consistently across kernels. Right now only flash path includes full NVTX.
- Correlate CPU-thread wait-times with GPU kernel start times (traceplay already, but need automated post-processor that prints summary table).

Edge cases and failure modes observed:
- OOM recoveries on paged path sometimes invisible in runtime logs because driver reclaimed pages asynchronously; need explicit page-fault hooks and alerting.
- Quantized fusedops (int8) shows larger variability when sequence mix changes — likely rounding introduced extra memory traffic patterns.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- (Aisha) Land the hysteresis config flag behind runtime feature flag + unit tests (Jira INF-2173). Target patch: small config + metrics. ETA: 1 week.
- (Kevin) Add nvtx for handshake & kv-alloc in all kernel code paths; update traceplay postprocessor to generate a one-page summary. ETA: 2 weeks.
- (Mariana) Run a two-day soak with 1% long-spike traffic on canary cluster, collect prometheus + traces. Focus on p99 regressions and any memory growth. ETA: 3 weeks.

Open questions to decide in design review:
- What default hysteresis parameters for hosted vs dedicated tiers? (Sensible default vs conservative for enterprise?)
- Should we add explicit pre-warm api to client to declare upcoming long-context requests? (Tooling vs runtime inference)

Attachment pointers (in artifacts folder): traceplay_1709410201.nsight, perf-summaries/short-heavy-batch8.csv, hybrid-fallback-logs/2026-02-16.log

Notes-to-self / quick checklist before PR:
- add unit test for fallback window boundaries
- add e2e soak job in infra that can replay mixed seq workload using stored traces
- sanity-check memory accounting metrics against nvidia-smi every 30s in soak runs

Appendix (raw sample numbers):
- mixed batch=8: fusedops steady tokens/sec 12.4k, flash 11.1k, hybrid 11.7k. p50/p95/p99 fusedops 9/34/45ms, flash 12/41/60ms, hybrid 11/29/28ms.
- short-heavy batch=8: fusedops p99 18ms (tokens/sec 14.8k)
- long-spike batch=1: flash p99 190ms (single long-request optimized path), fusedops p99 275ms due to fallback stall.

If anyone else wants to pick this up, read the traces under /tmp/attn_play/ and start from the hybrid run; the trace IDs are embedded in the log headers.

End of notes.
